payload.rationale: Historically, the US has not seen more than 6,000 measles cases in a single year since endemic transmission was declared eliminated in 2000. The largest recent outbreak was in 2019, with 1,282 cases. Reaching 6,000 cases would require an unprecedented breakdown in herd immunity and multiple large, sustained outbreaks across the country. While vaccine hesitancy has increased in some communities, the baseline national vaccination rate remains high enough to prevent outbreaks of this magnitude under normal circumstances. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that the US public health infrastructure and baseline vaccination rates are robust enough that even severe outbreaks are contained well below 6,000 cases, making the true probability effectively zero. The strongest reason the estimate could be too low is if a sudden, severe drop in vaccination rates combined with a highly infectious imported strain sparked a nationwide outbreak that overwhelmed containment efforts, especially if public health responses were delayed or underfunded.
limitations: No current data for 2026 is available.
Relies entirely on historical base rates prior to the knowledge cutoff.
